claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) caused 1.6 million deaths in 2017.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of human tuberculosis (TB), caused 1.6 million deaths in 2017, and it is estimated that 23% of the world's population has a latent TB infection.
evidence: This is a factual statement about TB mortality statistics that is directly stated in the introduction.

claim: 23% of the world's population has a latent TB infection.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of human tuberculosis (TB), caused 1.6 million deaths in 2017, and it is estimated that 23% of the world's population has a latent TB infection.
evidence: This is a factual statement about TB prevalence that is directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Mtb's capacity to import and metabolize host-derived lipids, including fatty acids (FAs) and cholesterol, contributes to long-term persistence in vivo.
source: In particular, Mtb's capacity to import and metabolize host-derived lipids, including fatty acids (FAs) and cholesterol, contributes to long-term persistence in vivo (Nazarova et al., 2017; Nazarova et al., 2019; Pandey and Sassetti, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Mtb infection triggers the formation of lipid droplets (LDs) whose FA content was proposed to serve as a nutrient source for intracellular Mtb.
source: At the macrophage level, Mtb infection triggers the formation of lipid droplets (LDs) whose FA content was proposed to serve as a nutrient source for intracellular Mtb (Daniel et al., 2011; Peyron et al., 2008; Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: IFNγ promotes LD accumulation by Mtb-infected macrophages while impairing the pathogen's capacity to acquire host-derived FAs.
source: However, this view was challenged by a recent study showing that the IFNγ cytokine promotes LD accumulation by Mtb-infected macrophages while impairing the pathogen's capacity to acquire host-derived FAs (Knight et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: Mtb imports fluorescently labeled saturated and monounsaturated fatty acids (SFAs and MUFAs) via a dedicated protein machinery named Mce1.
source: Mtb was shown to import fluorescently labeled saturated and monounsaturated fatty acids (SFAs and MUFAs, respectively) via a dedicated protein machinery named Mce1, which is coordinated with Mce4-mediated import of cholesterol and plays an important role in Mtb lipid homeostasis (Laval et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2013; Nazarova et al., 2017; Nazarova et al., 2019; Wilburn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Mce1 is coordinated with Mce4-mediated import of cholesterol and plays an important role in Mtb lipid homeostasis.
source: Mtb was shown to import fluorescently labeled saturated and monounsaturated fatty acids (SFAs and MUFAs, respectively) via a dedicated protein machinery named Mce1, which is coordinated with Mce4-mediated import of cholesterol and plays an important role in Mtb lipid homeostasis (Laval et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2013; Nazarova et al., 2017; Nazarova et al., 2019; Wilburn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The catabolism of arachidonic acid (AA) by cyclooxygenases (COX) and lipoxygenases (LOX) yields prostaglandins and lipoxins/leukotrienes.
source: In particular, the catabolism of arachidonic acid (AA) by cyclooxygenases (COX) and lipoxygenases (LOX) yields prostaglandins and lipoxins/leukotrienes, products referred to as eicosanoids that are important signaling molecules modulating inflammation and apoptosis.
evidence: This is a statement about biochemical pathways that is directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Eicosanoids are important signaling molecules modulating inflammation and apoptosis.
source: In particular, the catabolism of arachidonic acid (AA) by cyclooxygenases (COX) and lipoxygenases (LOX) yields prostaglandins and lipoxins/leukotrienes, products referred to as eicosanoids that are important signaling molecules modulating inflammation and apoptosis.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological function of eicosanoids that is directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) induce signal-specific reprogramming of FA synthesis in macrophages, with differential impact on antibacterial immunity.
source: Interestingly, Toll-like receptors (TLRs) induce signal-specific reprogramming of FA synthesis in macrophages, with differential impact on antibacterial immunity (Hsieh et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: Mtb triggered a significant increase in intracellular levels of free SFA palmitic acid (PA) and MUFAs (oleic acid [OA] and vaccenic acid [VA]) after 24 hr.
source: Mtb triggered a significant increase in intracellular levels of free SFA palmitic acid (PA) and MUFAs (oleic acid [OA] and vaccenic acid [VA]) after 24 hr (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Mtb infection increased the level of the ω6 precursor linoleic acid (LA) and its conversion product dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA), but not the DGLA product AA.
source: With regard to PUFAs, we detected an increased level of the ω6 precursor linoleic acid (LA) that was associated with elevated levels of its conversion product dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA), but not the DGLA product AA (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Long-chain ω3 PUFAs docosapentaenoic acid (DPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) were not modulated by Mtb infection.
source: On the ω3 PUFA side, α-linolenic acid (ALA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) were below detection limit, and the low levels of long-chain ω3 PUFAs docosapentaenoic acid (DPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) were not modulated by Mtb infection (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Infection-driven variations in free FA levels were associated with parallel trends in total FA levels.
source: Infection-driven variations in free FA levels were associated with parallel trends in total FA levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: BMDM infection with the Mycobacterium bovis BCG vaccine induced comparable FA profiles to Mtb infection.
source: These changes were not specific of the Mtb pathogen as BMDM infection with the Mycobacterium bovis BCG vaccine induced comparable FA profiles (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and they were no longer observed 48 hr post infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mtb-driven changes in FA levels were no longer observed 48 hr post infection.
source: These changes were not specific of the Mtb pathogen as BMDM infection with the Mycobacterium bovis BCG vaccine induced comparable FA profiles (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and they were no longer observed 48 hr post infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stimulation of BMDMs with TLR2/4 agonists resulted in similar modulation of free and total FAs as Mtb infection.
source: When we stimulated BMDMs with TLR2/4 agonists, levels of free and total FAs were similarly modulated (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Mtb-driven changes in FA levels in host macrophages result from recognition of mycobacteria pattern by TLR2/4.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mtb-driven changes in FA levels in host macrophages result from recognition of mycobacteria pattern by TLR2/4.
source: When we stimulated BMDMs with TLR2/4 agonists, levels of free and total FAs were similarly modulated (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Mtb-driven changes in FA levels in host macrophages result from recognition of mycobacteria pattern by TLR2/4.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TLR2/4 agonists produce similar effects to Mtb infection.

claim: De novo synthesis of SFAs is controlled by the FASN rate-limiting enzyme.
source: De novo synthesis of SFAs is controlled by the FASN rate-limiting enzyme, and MUFAs are generated from SFAs by the SCD2 rate-limiting enzyme (Figure 1A; Guillou et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: MUFAs are generated from SFAs by the SCD2 rate-limiting enzyme.
source: De novo synthesis of SFAs is controlled by the FASN rate-limiting enzyme, and MUFAs are generated from SFAs by the SCD2 rate-limiting enzyme (Figure 1A; Guillou et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: Increased levels of SFAs in Mtb-infected BMDMs were associated with upregulation of Fasn transcript levels from 6 hr post infection.
source: In Mtb-infected BMDMs, increased levels of SFAs were associated with upregulation of Fasn transcript levels from 6 hr post infection (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Scd2 mRNA expression was upregulated at 24 hr post infection with Mtb.
source: Scd2 mRNA expression was upregulated at 24 hr post infection with Mtb (Figure 2A), and the OA:SA ratio reflecting the efficacy of SFA conversion into MUFAs was increased upon Mtb and BCG infection (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The OA:SA ratio reflecting the efficacy of SFA conversion into MUFAs was increased upon Mtb and BCG infection.
source: Scd2 mRNA expression was upregulated at 24 hr post infection with Mtb (Figure 2A), and the OA:SA ratio reflecting the efficacy of SFA conversion into MUFAs was increased upon Mtb and BCG infection (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Conversion of ω6 and ω3 PUFA precursors into downstream PUFAs is jointly controlled by three enzymes: the FA desaturases (FADS)1 and FADS2, and the elongase ELOVL5.
source: Conversion of ω6 and ω3 PUFA precursors into downstream PUFAs is jointly controlled by three enzymes: the FA desaturases (FADS)1 and FADS2, and the elongase ELOVL5 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statement about biochemical pathways that is directly stated in the results.

claim: Fads1 and Elovl5 transcript levels were transiently repressed at 6hr post infection with Mtb.
source: Fads1 and Elovl5 transcript levels were transiently repressed at 6hr post infection with Mtb, while on the opposite those of Fads2 were increased from 6hr until 24hr (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Fads2 transcript levels were increased from 6hr until 24hr post infection with Mtb.
source: Fads1 and Elovl5 transcript levels were transiently repressed at 6hr post infection with Mtb, while on the opposite those of Fads2 were increased from 6hr until 24hr (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The transient downregulation of Fads1 and Elovl5 gene expression correlated with a drop in LXR activity, reflected by decreased transcript levels of LXR target gene Abca1 after 6 hr of Mtb infection.
source: It is interesting to note that the transient downregulation of Fads1 and Elovl5 gene expression correlated with a drop in LXR activity, reflected by decreased transcript levels of LXR target gene Abca1 after 6 hr of Mtb infection, despite significant induction of Nr1h3 gene expression.
evidence: This claim is based on correlation observed in the experimental data.

claim: The sustained upregulation of Fasn and Fads2 gene expression was associated with transcriptional induction of Srebf1 and its target gene Dhcr24.
source: The sustained upregulation of Fasn and Fads2 gene expression was associated with transcriptional induction of Srebf1 and its target gene Dhcr24 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mtb infection upregulates the biosynthesis of SFAs, MUFAs, and upstream PUFAs in host macrophages through activation of TLR2/4.
source: Together, data in Figures 1 and 2 indicate that Mtb infection upregulates the biosynthesis of SFAs, MUFAs, and upstream PUFAs in host macrophages through activation of TLR2/4.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: FA production results from activation of SREBP1.
source: They suggest that FA production results from activation of SREBP1, and that PUFA biosynthesis blockade downstream of FADS1 is due to a transient, post-transcriptional repression of LXR activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on gene expression.

claim: PUFA biosynthesis blockade downstream of FADS1 is due to a transient, post-transcriptional repression of LXR activity.
source: They suggest that FA production results from activation of SREBP1, and that PUFA biosynthesis blockade downstream of FADS1 is due to a transient, post-transcriptional repression of LXR activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on gene expression.

claim: Macrophage ability to mount efficient anti-Mtb responses relies on their activation by the Th1 cell-derived cytokine IFNγ.
source: Macrophage ability to mount efficient anti-Mtb responses relies on their activation by the Th1 cell-derived cytokine IFNγ, recently shown to limit host FA intake by intracellular Mtb (Knight et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: IFNγ limits host FA intake by intracellular Mtb.
source: Macrophage ability to mount efficient anti-Mtb responses relies on their activation by the Th1 cell-derived cytokine IFNγ, recently shown to limit host FA intake by intracellular Mtb (Knight et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: Stimulating BMDMs with IFNγ prior to infection prevented Mtb-induced expression of Fasn and Scd2.
source: Stimulating BMDMs with IFNγ prior to infection prevented Mtb-induced expression of Fasn and Scd2 (Figure 2A and C), suggesting that IFNγ limits de novo synthesis of SFAs and MUFAs by infected macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: IFNγ limits de novo synthesis of SFAs and MUFAs by infected macrophages.
source: Stimulating BMDMs with IFNγ prior to infection prevented Mtb-induced expression of Fasn and Scd2 (Figure 2A and C), suggesting that IFNγ limits de novo synthesis of SFAs and MUFAs by infected macrophages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on gene expression.

claim: IFNγ mitigated both the inhibitory effect of Mtb infection on Elovl5 and Fads1 gene expression after 6 hr, and its stimulatory effect on Fads2 gene expression.
source: The effect of IFNγ on PUFA biosynthetic enzymes was more complex as the cytokine mitigated both the inhibitory effect of Mtb infection on Elovl5 and Fads1 gene expression after 6 hr, and its stimulatory effect on Fads2 gene expression (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: IFNγ-induced decrease in Fasn and Fads2 expression correlated with reduced Abca1 and Dhcr24 transcript levels after 6 hr of infection.
source: IFNγ-induced decrease in Fasn and Fads2 expression correlated with reduced Abca1 and Dhcr24 transcript levels after 6 hr of infection (Figure 2D), suggesting that IFNγ prevents Mtb-induced stimulation of FA biosynthesis through downregulation of LXR and SREBP1 activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: IFNγ prevents Mtb-induced stimulation of FA biosynthesis through downregulation of LXR and SREBP1 activity.
source: IFNγ-induced decrease in Fasn and Fads2 expression correlated with reduced Abca1 and Dhcr24 transcript levels after 6 hr of infection (Figure 2D), suggesting that IFNγ prevents Mtb-induced stimulation of FA biosynthesis through downregulation of LXR and SREBP1 activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on gene expression.

claim: FADS2 activity was not modulated by Mtb in the conditions of the experiment.
source: FADS2 activity was not modulated by Mtb in the conditions of the experiment, suggesting that infection-induced upregulation of Fads2 expression (Figure 2C) takes more than 24 hr to translate into enhanced enzyme activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the FADS2 activity assay.

claim: Infection-induced upregulation of Fads2 expression takes more than 24 hr to translate into enhanced enzyme activity.
source: FADS2 activity was not modulated by Mtb in the conditions of the experiment, suggesting that infection-induced upregulation of Fads2 expression (Figure 2C) takes more than 24 hr to translate into enhanced enzyme activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that gene expression changes did not correlate with enzyme activity changes.

claim: Decreased Fads1 expression at 6 hr post infection correlated with a marked reduction of FADS1-mediated conversion of DGLA in AA.
source: In contrast, decreased Fads1 expression at 6 hr post infection (Figure 2C) correlated with a marked reduction of FADS1-mediated conversion of DGLA in AA (Figure 3A), irrespective of IFNγ stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 3A.

claim: IFNγ-driven repression of Fads2 gene expression in Mtb-infected BMDMs resulted in potent suppression of FADS2 activity.
source: Likewise, IFNγ-driven repression of Fads2 gene expression in Mtb-infected BMDMs (Figure 2C) resulted in potent suppression of FADS2 activity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 3A.

claim: Neither Mtb infection nor IFNγ stimulation affected the activity of ELOVL5.
source: Neither Mtb infection nor IFNγ stimulation affected the activity of ELOVL5.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the enzyme activity assay.

claim: IFNγ shuts down the biosynthesis of all FAs in Mtb-infected macrophages.
source: Therefore, the partial upregulation of the PUFA biosynthetic pathway that we observed in Mtb-infected macrophages was abrogated by cell exposure to IFNγ. In all, these results indicated that IFNγ shuts down the biosynthesis of all FAs in Mtb-infected macrophages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on FA biosynthesis.

claim: BMDMs infected with Mtb upregulated Ptgs2 expression.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Chen et al., 2008; Knight et al., 2018), BMDMs infected with Mtb upregulated Ptgs2 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and secreted higher amounts of AA metabolites deriving from both the COX (Figure 3C) and LOX pathways (Figure 3D) compared to noninfected controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and citations to previous studies.

claim: BMDMs infected with Mtb secreted higher amounts of AA metabolites deriving from both the COX and LOX pathways compared to noninfected controls.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Chen et al., 2008; Knight et al., 2018), BMDMs infected with Mtb upregulated Ptgs2 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and secreted higher amounts of AA metabolites deriving from both the COX (Figure 3C) and LOX pathways (Figure 3D) compared to noninfected controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3D and citations to previous studies.

claim: When BMDMs were infected with Mtb in the presence of iFADS2, the production of all COX/LOX-derived AA metabolites was significantly reduced.
source: When BMDMs were infected with Mtb in the presence of iFADS2, the production of all COX/LOX-derived AA metabolites was significantly reduced (Figure 3C and D), suggesting that part of the infection-induced eicosanoids may originate from de novo synthesized PUFAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Part of the infection-induced eicosanoids may originate from de novo synthesized PUFAs.
source: When BMDMs were infected with Mtb in the presence of iFADS2, the production of all COX/LOX-derived AA metabolites was significantly reduced (Figure 3C and D), suggesting that part of the infection-induced eicosanoids may originate from de novo synthesized PUFAs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that FADS2 inhibition reduces eicosanoid production.

claim: Upregulation of Ptgs2 expression and production of PGE2 were both potentiated by BMDM exposure to IFNγ prior to infection with Mtb.
source: Of note, upregulation of Ptgs2 expression and production of PGE2 were both potentiated by BMDM exposure to IFNγ prior to infection with Mtb, and the inhibitory effect of iFADS2 on Mtb-driven production of PGE2 production was maintained in IFNγ-activated macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The inhibitory effect of iFADS2 on Mtb-driven production of PGE2 was maintained in IFNγ-activated macrophages.
source: Of note, upregulation of Ptgs2 expression and production of PGE2 were both potentiated by BMDM exposure to IFNγ prior to infection with Mtb, and the inhibitory effect of iFADS2 on Mtb-driven production of PGE2 production was maintained in IFNγ-activated macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: PGE2 and LXA4 production by infected macrophages differentially influence the outcome of Mtb infection, promoting anti- or pro-mycobacterial responses via the induction of apoptotic or necrotic cell death, respectively.
source: PGE2 and LXA4 production by infected macrophages differentially influence the outcome of Mtb infection, promoting anti- or pro-mycobacterial responses via the induction of apoptotic or necrotic cell death, respectively (Chen et al., 2008; Divangahi et al., 2010; Mayer-Barber and Sher, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Cell apoptosis and expression of Syt7 were both downregulated by iFADS2 in Mtb-infected BMDMs, while necrosis levels remained unchanged.
source: Cell apoptosis and expression of Syt7, which is involved in lysosome-mediated membrane repair, were both downregulated by iFADS2 in Mtb-infected BMDMs, while necrosis levels remained unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: iFADS2-induced alterations of the PGE2/LXA4 balance results in a modest impairment of macrophage membrane repair and apoptosis during Mtb infection.
source: We concluded that iFADS2-induced alterations of the PGE2/LXA4 balance results in a modest impairment of macrophage membrane repair and apoptosis during Mtb infection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on apoptosis and necrosis.

claim: FADS2 inhibition induced a decrease in Ptgs2 gene expression in iFADS2-treated BMDMs infected with Mtb.
source: We detected a decrease in Ptgs2 gene expression in iFADS2-treated BMDMs infected with Mtb, which may account for the observed decrease in PGE2 production (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from NanoString analysis.

claim: FADS2 inhibition induced a significant downregulation of major inflammatory genes (Tnf, Il1b, Il6).
source: Besides, FADS2 inhibition induced a significant downregulation of major inflammatory genes (Tnf, Il1b, Il6) (Figure 3E) and genes involved in antimicrobial responses of macrophages (Nos2, Nox1, Irg1, Sod2) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: FADS2 inhibition induced a significant downregulation of genes involved in antimicrobial responses of macrophages (Nos2, Nox1, Irg1, Sod2).
source: Besides, FADS2 inhibition induced a significant downregulation of major inflammatory genes (Tnf, Il1b, Il6) (Figure 3E) and genes involved in antimicrobial responses of macrophages (Nos2, Nox1, Irg1, Sod2) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The PUFA biosynthetic pathway promotes antimicrobial and inflammatory responses.
source: Overall, our analyses of FADS2-inhibited macrophages indicated that the PUFA biosynthetic pathway promotes antimicrobial and inflammatory responses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on gene expression and eicosanoid production.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of FADS2 had no detectable effect on intracellular growth of Mtb in resting or IFNγ-stimulated BMDMs.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of FADS2 had no detectable effect on intracellular growth of Mtb (Figure 4A), neither in resting nor IFNγ-stimulated BMDMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mtb grew similarly in wild-type (WT) and FADS2 knock-out (KO) THP-1 clones.
source: In line with our data using iFADS2 and siRNAs, Mtb grew similarly in wild-type (WT) and knock-out (KO) clones (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mouse treatment with iFADS2 did not significantly alter Mtb growth in lungs and spleen in the conditions tested.
source: Mouse treatment with iFADS2 did not significantly alter Mtb growth in lungs and spleen in the conditions tested (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: iFADS2 treatment altered the transcriptional induction of inflammatory (Il1b, Il6, Tnf) and antimicrobial (Ptgs2, Nos2, Ch25h) genes in lungs of Mtb-infected mice.
source: However, iFADS2 treatment altered the transcriptional induction of inflammatory (Il1b, Il6, Tnf) and antimicrobial (Ptgs2, Nos2, Ch25h) genes in lungs of Mtb-infected mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: FADS2 promotes the generation of anti-mycobacterial responses.
source: In line with our data obtained in macrophages, these results indicated that FADS2 promotes the generation of anti-mycobacterial responses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on gene expression in infected mice.

claim: Blocking PUFA biosynthesis in infected hosts was not sufficient to impair Mtb growth.
source: Blocking PUFA biosynthesis in infected hosts was nevertheless not sufficient to impair Mtb growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mouse infection model.

claim: SFAs and MUFAs like PA and OA are readily imported and metabolized by Mtb in axenic cultures and within macrophages.
source: Indeed, SFAs and MUFAs like PA and OA have been shown to be readily imported and metabolized by Mtb in axenic cultures and within macrophages (Nazarova et al., 2017; Nazarova et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: PA and OA are efficiently internalized by Mtb.
source: Using this approach, we confirmed that PA, and OA to a lower extent, are efficiently internalized by Mtb (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ω3 PUFAs (EPA and DHA) uptake by Mtb was barely detected.
source: While ω3 PUFAs (EPA and DHA) uptake was barely detected, we found that ω6 PUFAs (LA and AA) were imported by Mtb as efficiently as OA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the alkyne-FA uptake assay.

claim: ω6 PUFAs (LA and AA) were imported by Mtb as efficiently as OA.
source: While ω3 PUFAs (EPA and DHA) uptake was barely detected, we found that ω6 PUFAs (LA and AA) were imported by Mtb as efficiently as OA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the alkyne-FA uptake assay.

claim: Knocking out lucA, mce1D, or yrbE1A, but not yrbE2A, yrbE3A, or yrbE4A, resulted in pronounced defects in alkyne-PA and -OA import.
source: In accordance with previous studies (Nazarova et al., 2017; Nazarova et al., 2019), knocking out lucA, mce1D, or yrbE1A, but not yrbE2A, yrbE3A, or yrbE4A, resulted in pronounced defects in alkyne-PA and -OA import (as shown for PA in Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Mtb's import of alkyne-LA, -AA, -EPA, and -DHA was abrogated in the ΔyrbE1A and Δmce1D mutants.
source: Likewise, we found that Mtb's import of alkyne-LA, -AA, -EPA, and -DHA was abrogated in the ΔyrbE1A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and Δmce1D mutants (Figure 5E), and that FA import was restored in the Δmce1D::comp complemented strain (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FA import was restored in the Δmce1D::comp complemented strain.
source: Likewise, we found that Mtb's import of alkyne-LA, -AA, -EPA, and -DHA was abrogated in the ΔyrbE1A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and Δmce1D mutants (Figure 5E), and that FA import was restored in the Δmce1D::comp complemented strain (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mtb has the ability to import PUFAs via the Mce1 transporter.
source: This established Mtb's ability to import PUFAs via the Mce1 transporter.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on mutant strains.

claim: Uptake of alkyne-OA, -LA, and -AA was dose-dependently decreased by addition of their natural counterpart.
source: Uptake of alkyne-OA, -LA, and -AA was dose-dependently decreased by addition of their natural counterpart, validating the conditions of the assay (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: LA and AA competed with each other and with OA, but not with PA.
source: Interestingly, LA and AA competed with each other and with OA, but not with PA (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SFAs, MUFAs, and ω6 PUFAs are imported by Mtb via Mce1 in axenic culture, with variable efficacy.
source: Together, data in Figure 5 indicated that SFAs, MUFAs, and ω6 PUFAs are imported by Mtb via Mce1 in axenic culture, with variable efficacy.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: ω6 PUFAs compete with OA, but not PA, for uptake by Mce1.
source: They suggested that ω6 PUFAs compete with OA, but not PA, for uptake by Mce1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the competition assay data.

claim: All alkyne-FAs could be detected in intracellular Mtb after 24 hr, and at lower levels after 72 hr.
source: All alkyne-FAs could be detected in intracellular Mtb after 24 hr, and at lower levels after 72 hr (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Intracellular Mtb showed a marked preference for AA over all other FAs including PA.
source: Differently from in vitro grown Mtb (Figure 5B), intracellular Mtb showed a marked preference for AA over all other FAs including PA (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Bacterial import of AA was significantly decreased by IFNγ priming.
source: After 24 hr of infection, Mtb's uptake of PA, OA, LA, and EPA was comparable in resting and IFNγ-activated BMDMs. However, bacterial import of AA was significantly decreased by IFNγ priming (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Increased uptake of AA by intracellular Mtb correlated with a relatively higher internalization of this FA by host macrophages, irrespective of Mtb infection.
source: It is interesting to note that increased uptake of AA by intracellular Mtb correlated with a relatively higher internalization of this FA by host macrophages, irrespective of Mtb infection (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: It is the intracellular bioavailability of AA that determines its import by Mtb, rather than intrinsic bacterial factors.
source: This finding suggested that it is the intracellular bioavailability of AA that determines its import by Mtb, rather than intrinsic bacterial factors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between macrophage and bacterial AA uptake.

claim: Mtb's import of PA and OA was decreased by approximately 40% in the absence of Mce1D and restored by gene complementation.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Nazarova et al., 2019), Mtb's import of PA and OA was decreased by approximately 40% in the absence of Mce1D and restored by gene complementation (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, and citations to previous studies.

claim: Mtb's import of LA and AA was reduced by mce1D gene knockout, but to lower levels compared to PA and OA.
source: Mtb's import of LA and AA was also reduced by mce1D gene knockout, but to lower levels compared to PA and OA (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The growth of the Δmce1D mutant significantly decelerated after 6 days compared to WT and complemented strains.
source: Although all strains displayed comparable intracellular growth during the first 3 days of BMDM infection (corresponding to the timeframe used in other experiments in this study), that of the Δmce1D mutant significantly decelerated after 6 days compared to WT and complemented strains (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Compared to WT Mtb, Δmce1D Mtb induced less COX-derived PGE2 and TXB2 and more LOX-derived 15-HETE and LXA4.
source: Compared to WT Mtb, Δmce1D Mtb induced less COX-derived PGE2 and TXB2 and more LOX-derived 15-HETE and LXA4 (Figure 6G), an eicosanoid profile that is considered pro-mycobacterial.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Transcriptional induction of key inflammatory genes including Pgts2 was significantly downregulated in macrophages infected with Δmce1D Mtb for 24 hr, compared to WT and complemented Mtb.
source: Furthermore, transcriptional induction of key inflammatory genes including Pgts2 was significantly downregulated in macrophages infected with Δmce1D Mtb for 24 hr, compared to WT and complemented Mtb (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In the context of macrophages Mtb preferentially imports AA over other host-derived FAs via mechanisms partially depending on the Mce1 transporter.
source: Together, our data in Figure 6 revealed that in the context of macrophages Mtb preferentially imports AA over other host-derived FAs via mechanisms partially depending on the Mce1 transporter.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Infection-induced mobilization of AA is opportunistically hijacked by Mtb to support intracellular growth.
source: Rather, they support the view that infection-induced mobilization of AA is opportunistically hijacked by Mtb to support intracellular growth.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on AA uptake and bacterial growth.

claim: Radiolabeled LA and ALA were incorporated into cell wall lipids of Mtb grown under axenic conditions.
source: Our findings are consistent with previous observations that radiolabeled LA and ALA were incorporated into cell wall lipids of Mtb grown under axenic conditions (Morbidoni et al., 2006), and that AA used as a sole carbon source was able to support Mtb growth in vitro (Forrellad et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: AA used as a sole carbon source was able to support Mtb growth in vitro.
source: Our findings are consistent with previous observations that radiolabeled LA and ALA were incorporated into cell wall lipids of Mtb grown under axenic conditions (Morbidoni et al., 2006), and that AA used as a sole carbon source was able to support Mtb growth in vitro (Forrellad et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: ω6 PUFAs were imported as efficiently as MUFAs and competed with MUFAs for Mce1-mediated import in Mtb.
source: ω6 PUFAs were imported as efficiently as MUFAs and competed with MUFAs for Mce1-mediated import in Mtb.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on FA uptake and competition.

claim: MUFAs and ω6 PUFAs share the same binding site on the Mce1 transporter or use a common accessory FA-binding protein that directs these FAs to the Mce1 transporter.
source: This suggests that MUFAs and ω6 PUFAs share the same binding site on the Mce1 transporter or use a common accessory FA-binding protein that directs these FAs to the Mce1 transporter.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the competition data.

claim: Mce1A-F proteins are believed to form a channel recognizing FA substrates and shuttling them across the mycobacterial cell wall to deliver them to the putative YrbE1A/B permeases embedded in the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: Based on Mce1 gene inactivation studies (Nazarova et al., 2019; Wilburn et al., 2018), Mce1A-F proteins are believed to form a channel recognizing FA substrates and shuttling them across the mycobacterial cell wall to deliver them to the putative YrbE1A/B permeases embedded in the cytoplasmic membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Mutations in the mce1D and yrbE1A genes reduce Mtb's import of PUFAs by more than 80% in vitro.
source: Our observation that mutations in the mce1D and yrbE1A genes reduce Mtb's import of PUFAs by more than 80% in vitro supports the view that these proteins play a critical role in recognition and internalization of PUFAs, similar to SFAs and MUFAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mutant strain analysis.

claim: The distinctive conformational properties of natural, cis ω3 PUFAs, such as high flexibility, may account for a lower affinity for the Mce1 receptor.
source: The distinctive conformational properties of natural, cis ω3 PUFAs, such as high flexibility, may account for a lower affinity for the Mce1 receptor (Chu and Wang, 2014).
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning supported by a citation.

claim: Mce1 displays at least two distinct FA-binding sites specialized in recognition of SFAs and MUFAs/PUFAs, respectively.
source: This suggests that Mce1 displays at least two distinct FA-binding sites specialized in recognition of SFAs and MUFAs/PUFAs, respectively, a property that may help Mtb optimize the uptake of host-derived FAs during infection.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the competition data.

claim: Mtb infection triggers an increase in intracellular levels of free SFAs and MUFAs preceded by an upregulation of Fasn gene expression in host macrophages.
source: Our lipidomic analyses demonstrated that Mtb infection triggers an increase in intracellular levels of free SFAs and MUFAs preceded by an upregulation of Fasn gene expression in host macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipidomic and gene expression analyses.

claim: Mtb represses the expression of Pparg and several PPARγ gene targets involved in FA catabolism (Cpt1a, Acox3, Lipa).
source: We also observed that Mtb represses the expression of Pparg and several PPARγ gene targets involved in FA catabolism (Cpt1a, Acox3, Lipa) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), which may further promote free SFA and MUFA accumulation in infected macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The MyD88 signaling pathway is a major driver of SFA and MUFA metabolism reprogramming in TLR2/4-stimulated macrophages.
source: Recent studies have identified the MyD88 signaling pathway as a major driver of SFA and MUFA metabolism reprogramming in TLR2/4-stimulated macrophages (Hsieh et al., 2020; Oishi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Recognition of Mtb pattern by TLR2/4 triggers SFA and MUFA biosynthesis.
source: Cellular levels of SFAs and MUFAs were increased in BMDMs stimulated with TLR2 or TLR4 agonists, supporting the hypothesis that recognition of Mtb pattern by these receptors triggers SFA and MUFA biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on TLR agonist stimulation.

claim: Total and free LA levels were upregulated by Mtb or TLR2 and TLR4 stimulation, suggesting an enhanced uptake of this essential ω6 PUFA precursor by host macrophages upon infection.
source: Likewise, total and free LA levels were upregulated by Mtb or TLR2 and TLR4 stimulation, suggesting an enhanced uptake of this essential ω6 PUFA precursor by host macrophages upon infection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on LA levels.

claim: A comparable blockade in long PUFA production by BMDMs stimulated with TLR2 or TLR4 agonists was detected in a recent lipidomic study.
source: These findings are corroborated by a recent lipidomic study that detected a comparable blockade in long PUFA production by BMDMs stimulated with TLR2 or TLR4 agonists (Hsieh et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: AA is mobilized from other sources to meet the cell's demands despite decreased biosynthesis.
source: Despite a decreased biosynthesis (Figure 3A), free and total AA levels were stable in Mtb-infected BMDMs (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), implying that AA is mobilized from other sources to meet the cell's demands.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that AA levels remain stable despite decreased biosynthesis.

claim: Macrophages import exogenous AA with a particularly high efficacy compared to other FAs.
source: Our studies of FA-pulsed BMDMs indicated that macrophages import exogenous AA with a particularly high efficacy compared to other FAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FA-pulsed macrophages.

claim: IFNγ priming of Mtb-infected macrophages fully blocked PUFA biosynthesis by downregulating Fads2 gene expression.
source: Importantly, IFNγ priming of Mtb-infected macrophages fully blocked PUFA biosynthesis by downregulating Fads2 gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on gene expression and enzyme activity.

claim: IFNγ selectively restricted AA import by intracellular Mtb.
source: In addition, IFNγ selectively restricted AA import by intracellular Mtb, suggesting that IFNγ signaling activates several mechanisms preventing the pathogen from hijacking this FA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on FA uptake by intracellular bacteria.

claim: IFNγ signaling activates several mechanisms preventing the pathogen from hijacking AA.
source: In addition, IFNγ selectively restricted AA import by intracellular Mtb, suggesting that IFNγ signaling activates several mechanisms preventing the pathogen from hijacking this FA.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data.

claim: The differential uptake of PA and AA by intracellular Mtb correlates with the relative abundance of these FAs in the macrophage cytosol.
source: Our observation that the differential uptake of PA and AA by intracellular Mtb correlates with the relative abundance of these FAs in the macrophage cytosol suggests that FA uptake by intracellular Mtb is primarily determined by their local bioavailability.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between macrophage and bacterial FA uptake.

claim: Intracellular persistence of the mce1D mutant of Mtb in macrophages was impaired at late stage of infection.
source: Interestingly, intracellular persistence of the mce1D mutant of Mtb in macrophages was impaired at late stage of infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on bacterial growth in macrophages.

claim: The Δmce1D mutant was a less good inducer of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids and cytokines in infected macrophages compared to WT Mtb.
source: This was not due to the generation of better anti-mycobacterial responses in host macrophages as compared to WT Mtb as the Δmce1D mutant was a less good inducer of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids and cytokines in infected macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on eicosanoid and cytokine production.

claim: Exogenous AA is superiorly imported by macrophages compared to other FAs.
source: Together with our observation that exogenous AA is superiorly imported by macrophages compared to other FAs, these findings support the view that Mce1-mediated import of AA plays an important role in Mtb survival within macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on FA uptake by macrophages.

claim: Mce1-mediated import of AA plays an important role in Mtb survival within macrophages.
source: Together with our observation that exogenous AA is superiorly imported by macrophages compared to other FAs, these findings support the view that Mce1-mediated import of AA plays an important role in Mtb survival within macrophages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on AA uptake and bacterial survival.

claim: The pro-inflammatory action of eicosanoids is beneficial to the host at early stages of infection by promoting the intracellular killing of Mtb via induction of TNFα in infected macrophages.
source: While the pro-inflammatory action of eicosanoids is beneficial to the host at early stages of infection by promoting the intracellular killing of Mtb via induction of TNFα in infected macrophages, it may drive immunopathology at later stages of disease (reviewed in Young et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Eicosanoids may drive immunopathology at later stages of TB disease.
source: While the pro-inflammatory action of eicosanoids is beneficial to the host at early stages of infection by promoting the intracellular killing of Mtb via induction of TNFα in infected macrophages, it may drive immunopathology at later stages of disease (reviewed in Young et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs inhibiting COX activity are being evaluated in humans as adjunctive therapies to standard TB treatments.
source: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs inhibiting COX activity are being evaluated in humans as adjunctive therapies to standard TB treatments, with the rationale to limit inflammation-induced tissue pathology.
evidence: This is a statement about current clinical research that is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: Transcriptional repression of Fads1 in Mtb-infected macrophages did not prevent the production of AA-derived secondary metabolites, especially the pro-inflammatory COX products PGE2, PGD2, and TXB2.
source: In our study, transcriptional repression of Fads1 in Mtb-infected macrophages did not prevent the production of AA-derived secondary metabolites, especially the pro-inflammatory COX products PGE2, PGD2, and TXB2 (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Inhibiting FADS2 had a global anti-inflammatory effect during Mtb infection both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Inhibiting FADS2 had a global anti-inflammatory effect during Mtb infection both in vitro and in vivo, which was associated with induction of a pro-mycobacterial eicosanoid profile in infected macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro and in vivo studies.

claim: Inhibiting FADS2 was associated with induction of a pro-mycobacterial eicosanoid profile in infected macrophages.
source: Inhibiting FADS2 had a global anti-inflammatory effect during Mtb infection both in vitro and in vivo, which was associated with induction of a pro-mycobacterial eicosanoid profile in infected macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on eicosanoid production.

claim: iFADS2 may increase the efficacy of COX inhibitors in immunopathological conditions, while depriving Mtb of additional FA sources.
source: Therefore, iFADS2 may increase the efficacy of COX inhibitors in immunopathological conditions, while depriving Mtb of additional FA sources.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings.
